trimethoprim.name: Trimethoprim
trimethoprim.summary: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic used to treat and prevent urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and occasionally other infections. It interferes with folic acid production in bacteria, so folate-related cautions, including pregnancy, are a recurring theme in its patient information. The NHS lists blood and skin reactions as rare serious side effects that need prompt medical help.
trimethoprim.class: Antibacterial (folate pathway inhibitor), used for urinary tract infections
usedFor: Treating urinary tract infections, such as cystitis
Occasionally other infections, including chest infections and acne
trimethoprim.howItWorks: Trimethoprim works by interfering with the way bacteria make folic acid. Antibiotics such as this act on bacteria and do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections. In the body, a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels.

common: Itching or a mild rash, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, thrush and headaches are the common effects, reported in more than 1 in 100 people according to the NHS.
Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can stop contraceptive pills from protecting against pregnancy.
Everyday painkillers such as paracetamol and ibuprofen are described by the NHS as fine to take alongside trimethoprim.
serious: Unexplained bruising or bleeding, a sore throat, mouth ulcers or a fever can signal a blood problem and need prompt medical help (NHS 111 or the GP the same day).
Serious skin reactions such as blistering or peeling need prompt medical help (NHS 111 or the GP the same day).

Bloody or severe diarrhoea, severe stomach pain (which can signal pancreatitis) and yellowing of the skin or eyes (which can signal liver problems) are listed as serious effects needing prompt medical help.
Signs of meningitis, or of high potassium such as muscle weakness or an abnormal heartbeat, are emergencies: call 999 or go to A&E.
Swelling of the lips, mouth or throat, or difficulty breathing, may signal a serious allergic reaction and needs a 999 call.

cautions: The NHS lists past allergic reactions to trimethoprim or other medicines, liver or kidney problems, low folate levels, porphyria and other blood disorders among the reasons it may not suit a person.
Pregnancy and trying to conceive are circumstances where the NHS advises checking with a doctor first.
The NHS says trimethoprim can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in early pregnancy, because it can lower folic acid levels.
For someone trying to conceive who takes it daily, the NHS says the doctor may change the antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid.
Small amounts pass into breast milk and side effects in the baby are unlikely with short-term use, though a pharmacist, doctor, midwife or health visitor is the person to ask.
Medicines named by the NHS as interacting include rifampicin, warfarin, acenocoumarol, digoxin, phenytoin, repaglinide, pioglitazone and methotrexate.
The NHS says there is not enough information to say that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to combine with trimethoprim.
MedlinePlus asks people to tell the prescriber about allergies to trimethoprim or sulfa drugs and about all other medicines, vitamins and supplements.
trimethoprim.alcohol: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, but heavy drinking is best avoided.
trimethoprim.foodInteractions: The NHS says normal eating and drinking can continue during treatment.
trimethoprim.monitoring: The NHS pages reviewed describe no routine tests during a course of treatment. They note that a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels, and that a doctor may change the antibiotic or prescribe folic acid in some people who take it daily while trying to conceive.

sections.heading: What is trimethoprim used for?
sections.body: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS says it is used to treat and to prevent urinary tract infections, such as cystitis. Less often it is used for other infections, including chest infections and acne. NICE guidance on lower urinary tract infection names trimethoprim as one of two first-choice antibiotics, alongside nitrofurantoin. NICE adds that resistance to trimethoprim is high across the country, so it is considered when the individual risk of resistance is low. That risk may be higher after recent use of the antibiotic and in older people living in care homes. In men, NICE notes that trimethoprim can reach useful levels in prostate tissue. Antibiotics do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections, as the NHS points out.

sections.heading: How does trimethoprim work, and why does folic acid come up?
sections.body: Trimethoprim works by interfering with the way bacteria make folic acid. The NHS explains that a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels in the body. Folate is therefore a recurring theme in the patient information. Low folate levels appear on the NHS list of reasons why the medicine may not be suitable. The NHS also notes that the medicine can lower folic acid levels in pregnancy, which is why it is not usually recommended in early pregnancy. An NHS England case study describes spinal cord malformation in the foetus as a possible result of use in early pregnancy. For someone trying to conceive who takes the medicine daily, the NHS says the doctor may switch antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid. Antibiotics of this kind act on bacteria, which is why they have no effect on viruses.

sections.heading: What are the side effects, and which need urgent help?
sections.body: The NHS lists itching or a mild rash, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, thrush and headaches as common effects. Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can stop contraceptive pills from working. Unexplained bruising or bleeding, a sore throat, mouth ulcers or a fever can signal a blood problem. Blistering or peeling skin is a serious skin reaction. Bloody or severe diarrhoea, severe stomach pain and yellowing of the skin or eyes also need prompt medical help, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day. Signs of meningitis, high potassium (muscle weakness or an abnormal heartbeat) or a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the lips, mouth or throat, are emergencies: call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with trimethoprim?
sections.body: The NHS lists past allergic reactions to trimethoprim or other medicines, liver or kidney problems, low folate levels, porphyria and other blood disorders as reasons the medicine may not suit someone. MedlinePlus also asks people to tell the prescriber about allergies to trimethoprim or sulfa drugs. Pregnancy is another consideration. The NHS says trimethoprim can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in the early weeks. It says there is no evidence that the medicine affects fertility in men or women. For someone trying to conceive who takes it daily, a doctor may switch antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid. The NHS says small amounts pass into breast milk and that side effects in the baby are unlikely with short-term use.

sections.heading: Trimethoprim with other medicines, alcohol and food
sections.body: The NHS names several medicines that interact with trimethoprim and can raise the chance of side effects. These include rifampicin, warfarin, acenocoumarol, digoxin, phenytoin, repaglinide, pioglitazone and methotrexate. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are described as fine to take with it. For herbal remedies and supplements, the NHS says there is not enough information to know whether they can be combined with it. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, though heavy drinking is best avoided. Normal eating and drinking can continue. For sickness, the NHS suggests taking the tablets with or after food. Anyone taking several medicines, or taking vitamins and supplements, is asked by MedlinePlus to tell the prescriber, who may adjust doses or watch for side effects.

faqs.q: Can trimethoprim be taken during pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in early pregnancy, because it can lower folic acid levels. Anyone who is pregnant or trying to conceive is advised by the NHS to check with a doctor first. A doctor may choose a different antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid.

faqs.q: Why does folic acid matter with trimethoprim?
faqs.a: Trimethoprim interferes with folic acid production in bacteria, and a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels in the body. Low folate levels are on the NHS list of reasons the medicine may not suit someone, and early pregnancy is a time of particular care.

faqs.q: What side effects need urgent attention?
faqs.a: Unexplained bruising or bleeding, sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever, blistering or peeling skin and yellow skin or eyes need prompt medical help from NHS 111 or the GP the same day. Swelling of the lips, mouth or throat, difficulty breathing, muscle weakness or an abnormal heartbeat call for 999 or A&E.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking trimethoprim?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, but it is best not to drink too much. It also says normal eating and drinking can continue.

faqs.q: Does trimethoprim help with colds or flu?
faqs.a: No. The NHS notes that antibiotics do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections. Trimethoprim is mainly used to treat and prevent urinary tract infections, and sometimes chest infections and acne.
